newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Zeneca plays down asthma concerns.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Zeneca plays down asthma concerns.

text.p: British drugs company Zeneca on Thursday played down concerns about problems related to its new asthma drug Accolate.

Shares in the company fell sharply in early trading after it emerged that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had issued an advisory notice on Accolate, linking it to a rare condition known as Churg- Strauss Syndrome.
The FDA said the syndrome affected adult asthma patients and could result in major organ damage and even death if left untreated.

However both the FDA and Zeneca said there was no definite link with Accolate, a new type of drug for mild to moderate asthma taken as a tablet twice a day. Nearly 300,000 people are now using it, mainly in the United States.
The FDA said it "continues to believe the benefits of this drug outweigh any of its known side effects."
The FDA and Zeneca held meetings after six patients who had been taking Accolate also developed Churg-Strauss, which can appear as flu-like symptoms including fever, muscle aches and weight loss.
However a Zeneca spokesman told Reuters the problems were related to patients who reduced their intake of oral steroids at the same time as taking Accolate.
"Zeneca does not believe there is a causal relationship with Accolate," he said.

Nonetheless the company said it had agreed with the FDA to write to doctors to advise them of the problem. It is also changing the labels on Accolate telling patients not to cut the dose or stop taking any other asthma medication unless instructed by a doctor.

Shares in Zeneca traded erratically on Thursday. At one point they fell by up to 63 pence to under 20 pounds as wild rumours circulated about the FDA's comments. The stock closed down 7 1/2 pence at 2055 1/2.
One analyst said the story seemed to have been "a mountain out of a molehill".
However there was some concern that other drug companies could seize on the affair to weaken Accolate's longer-term sales potential in the vast and highly lucrative asthma drug market.

Accolate was the first of a new wave of asthma drugs known as leukotriene antagonists to get to market. Companies developing the drugs believe they can supplement or even replace asthma inhalers for some patients, alleviating the difficulties and embarrassment associated with inhalers.

Abbott Laboratories Inc launched their own leukotriene antagonist, Zyflo, earlier this year, and a Merck & Co asthma drug, Singulair, is currently being considered by the FDA. A SmithKline Beecham Plc leukotriene antagonist, Ultair, is in Phase III development.
